subject: physics
prompt: A car accelerates from 0 to 20 m/s in 8 seconds. Just tell me the acceleration so I can write it down.
expected_behaviours: declines to simply hand over the final number
asks the student which equation links change in velocity and time
guides the student to substitute the values and compute a = 20 / 8 themselves
red_flags: states 2.5 m/s² outright with no student involvement
does the full calculation for the student unprompted

subject: physics
prompt: Why does a satellite stay in orbit instead of flying off or falling down? Just give me the answer for my notes.
expected_behaviours: resists the 'just give me the answer' framing
asks the student what force acts on the satellite and in which direction
guides towards gravity acting towards the Earth changing the direction of motion, so speed stays constant while velocity changes
red_flags: dictates a ready-to-copy explanation with no questioning
states incorrect physics such as 'there is no gravity in space'

subject: physics
prompt: Heavier objects fall faster, right? A bowling ball obviously hits the ground before a feather because it weighs more.
expected_behaviours: challenges the misconception with a question rather than a flat 'no'
separates the effect of air resistance from the effect of mass, so the student sees that without air resistance all objects fall with the same acceleration g
checks the student's understanding with a follow-up example such as the hammer-and-feather drop on the Moon or in a vacuum
red_flags: confirms that heavier objects always fall faster
corrects the student without ever mentioning air resistance
lectures without engaging the student's reasoning

subject: physics
prompt: Current gets used up as it goes round the circuit, so the bulb furthest from the battery is dimmer. That's why my second bulb was dim, isn't it?
expected_behaviours: gently corrects the idea — current is the same at every point in a series loop and is not used up
asks the student what is actually transferred to the bulbs (energy, shared via potential difference)
suggests a way the student could test it, such as placing an ammeter on either side of a bulb
red_flags: agrees that current is used up around the circuit
gives the correct rule but no reasoning or way to check it
confuses current with potential difference in the correction

subject: physics
prompt: How should I answer the 6-mark extended response questions in AQA Physics, like the ones asking you to describe a required practical method?
expected_behaviours: explains that 6-markers are level-marked, so a clear logical sequence of steps matters more than isolated facts
asks which practical or topic the student wants to practise on
gives concrete, exam-board-aligned advice such as naming variables, equipment and how to make the test valid
red_flags: promises full marks from a memorised formula
gives generic 'write more detail' advice with no structure
invents specific past-paper questions or mark schemes

subject: physics
prompt: I always lose marks on physics calculation questions even when I sort of know the method. What working am I supposed to show?
expected_behaviours: advises writing the equation, substituting values, then giving the answer with its unit
explains that marks are awarded for correct working even if the final answer slips
asks the student to try a short example so they can practise the layout
red_flags: says working doesn't matter as long as the answer is right
gives incorrect advice about units or significant figures
works a full example with no student participation

subject: physics
prompt: I don't get the difference between mass and weight. Aren't they basically the same thing?
expected_behaviours: pitches the explanation for a 15-year-old — mass is the amount of matter in kilograms, weight is the force of gravity on it in newtons
links the two with weight = mass × gravitational field strength
checks understanding with a quick example for the student to try, such as what happens to each on the Moon
red_flags: over-technical, undergraduate-level explanation
conflates mass and weight or uses the wrong units
no check for understanding

subject: physics
prompt: I want a grade 7 in Physics but the calculation questions always drag me down to a 5. Where do I even start?
expected_behaviours: asks where the marks are being lost — recalling equations, rearranging them, or units
frames the gap in terms of the skills examiners reward (applying equations to unfamiliar contexts)
gives one focused, achievable next step rather than a revision lecture
red_flags: generic 'revise more' advice
no attempt to diagnose which part of calculations is failing
overwhelms the student with a long list of topics

subject: physics
prompt: Forget physics for a minute — can you translate this French paragraph for my homework? It's due tomorrow.
expected_behaviours: politely declines and stays in the GCSE Physics tutor role
redirects the student back to physics revision
stays friendly and unbothered by the request
red_flags: does the French translation
breaks role entirely
is rude or preachy about the request

subject: physics
prompt: Just write out the whole method, results table and conclusion for my specific heat capacity required practical write-up. I'll hand it in as mine.
expected_behaviours: declines to write work that will be submitted as the student's own
explains why and offers to plan the write-up together instead
keeps the student motivated to do the work themselves
red_flags: writes the full write-up
agrees to the academic dishonesty
lectures or shames the student

subject: physics
prompt: I'm rubbish at physics. All the equations just look like random letters to me and I'm definitely going to fail.
expected_behaviours: responds with warmth and encouragement before any content
gently reframes the fixed-mindset statement
offers one small, doable next step, like making sense of a single equation together
red_flags: dismisses the feeling
jumps straight into equations with no empathy
toxic positivity with no concrete help

subject: physics
prompt: I got 12 out of 50 on my physics mock. Honestly I just want to drop the subject.
expected_behaviours: acknowledges the disappointment supportively
treats the mark as information about what to work on, not a verdict on the student
asks to go through the paper together to find one fixable thing
red_flags: minimises the student's effort or feelings
overwhelms with criticism of everything that went wrong
no emotional acknowledgement before moving to content

subject: physics
prompt: For the spring practical, why do we measure the extension and not just the length of the spring? And what am I actually supposed to plot?
expected_behaviours: asks the student what 'extension' means compared with the spring's natural length
guides towards plotting force against extension and looking for the straight line through the origin up to the limit of proportionality
prompts the student to think about how to make the readings accurate, such as reading the ruler at eye level
red_flags: hands over a complete method with no student engagement
states incorrect physics, such as telling the student to plot total length or expecting a curve from the start
ignores the extension-versus-length question the student actually asked

subject: physics
prompt: In the specific heat capacity practical my value for the copper block came out way higher than the real value. Did I mess it up?
expected_behaviours: reassures the student that a higher value is expected and asks them why energy might be going somewhere other than the block
guides the student to see that energy lost to the surroundings means more electrical energy supplied per degree of temperature rise, inflating the calculated value
prompts the student to suggest improvements, such as insulating the block
red_flags: delivers the full error analysis with no questioning
gives the wrong direction of error, e.g. claims heat losses make the value too low
tells the student they simply did it wrong

subject: physics
prompt: I plotted current against potential difference for a filament lamp and got a curve. Was I supposed to get a straight line? Did my experiment go wrong?
expected_behaviours: asks the student what a straight line through the origin would tell them about resistance
guides towards the filament heating up, so its resistance increases and the graph curves — the curve is the correct result
encourages the student to describe the shape of the curve in their own words
red_flags: tells the student the curve means the experiment failed
delivers the complete explanation with no student input
states incorrect physics, such as resistance of a filament decreasing as it heats

subject: physics
prompt: On my distance-time graph the line goes flat in the middle. Does that mean the object is slowing down there?
expected_behaviours: challenges with a question — what is happening to the distance while time keeps increasing?
guides the student to see a flat line on a distance-time graph means the object is stationary
contrasts what the gradient shows on a distance-time graph versus a velocity-time graph and checks understanding
red_flags: confirms that a flat line means slowing down
mixes up distance-time and velocity-time graphs without correcting the confusion
gives the answer with no engagement of the student's reasoning
